collection.title: Made by hand in Odisha
collection.lead: A cut piece of cloth. A brush held close. A silver thread bent into a pattern. Follow three crafts into the decisions—and the people—behind them.
collection.intro: Begin with an object that makes you stop. Stay for the question you want to ask its maker. This collection connects three traditions through photographs, sourced introductions and invitations to look more closely.

cards.title: Pipili · colour at the stitched edge
cards.text: Look at how separate shapes become a pattern, and how the maker’s tools bring them together.

cards.title: Pattachitra · read the painted line
cards.text: Begin with a small figure and let the border guide you towards its story.

cards.title: Cuttack · follow a silver thread
cards.text: Notice the spaces between the lines. Continue into the existing Tarakasi guide.

questions.heading: Notice
questions.text: Choose one edge, join or repeated motif. What makes you want a closer look?

questions.heading: Ask
questions.text: Who made this piece? Which stages did they work on? How did they learn?

questions.heading: Remember
questions.text: Ask for the maker’s preferred credit and permission before recording or sharing their story.

collection.limits: Three selected traditions, not a complete craft catalogue or an inspected workshop directory. The craft journey is a reading and planning collection; no day route, appointment, transfer or price has been verified.

pages.title: Pipili appliqué
pages.lead: Colour catches your eye. A seam holds it there. Look closely at the cut cloth, the stitched edge and the person who brings the pattern together.

sections.title: Follow a shape to its edge

paragraphs.text: Start with one circle in the photograph. Follow its outline, then look for the smaller shapes inside it. The pleasure is in discovering that the pattern is built from pieces.
The NID account hosted by D’source describes coloured fabric being cut into shapes and stitched into appliqué cloth. It also documents decorative stitching and added embellishments.
In the documented lampshade process, a stencil helps repeat the shape; cut pieces are organised before stitching. The account includes machine stitching as well as needlework.

Notice the sewing machine in Andrew Moore’s photograph. “Made by hand” here means attending to the maker’s work and decisions; it is not a promise that every stitch is hand-sewn. Ask which stages the person does and which tools they use.

Odisha Tourism connects Pipili appliqué with the decoration of Jagannath’s chariots during Ratha Yatra. It also lists wall hangings, lanterns, umbrellas, bags and bedspreads among the forms visitors may encounter.

A ritual canopy and a bag can lead to different conversations. Ask what this object was made for, where its pattern came from and whether the maker gives it a particular name. The photograph alone cannot identify a ceremonial use.

sections.title: A visit begins with a greeting

paragraphs.text: A shop display may be open to view while a workspace is busy. Ask whether the maker has time to speak. Agree the time and any fee before a demonstration; ask separately before photographing a person, an object or a workspace.
Confirm an exact meeting point, opening arrangements, steps, seating and toilets with your chosen host. No workshop appointment, demonstration or access inspection has been arranged by Utkal.

If you buy directly, ask who made the piece and which parts they worked on. Look at the edges together; ask about the fabric, lining, care and packing. A photograph cannot certify fibre, workmanship or durability.

Keep the maker’s preferred credit and a receipt. Agree the size, design, price and delivery terms before commissioning work. Ask separately about permission to share images of the work. A smaller piece with a story you understand can be a more lasting memory than a hurried purchase.

pages.title: Pattachitra · a story in the line
pages.lead: Before you try to understand the whole painting, follow one line. A border, a gesture, a tiny face can open a much larger story.

sections.title: Let the border lead you in

paragraphs.text: Look beside the artist’s brush. A small figure sits inside an arch; nearby, another border turns the corner. Try following the pattern with your eye before asking the artist where the story begins.
Odisha Tourism describes Pattachitra as painting on cloth and connects Raghurajpur’s work with Jagannath traditions and scenes from mythology and the epics.

sections.title: A surface made ready for a story

paragraphs.text: The Government of Odisha’s account describes cloth prepared with chalk and tamarind-seed glue, followed by the border, brush drawing, flat colour and fine dark outlines. This is a documented traditional process, not a specification for every piece sold today.

Ask whether you may see an unfinished surface beside a finished one. Which stage takes the most concentration? Which mark would the artist ask you to notice? Those answers belong to the person making this work.

sections.title: Ask what this particular picture tells

paragraphs.text: The government account names religious, mythological and folk themes, including Krishna and Jagannath. It also describes painted objects and palm-leaf works alongside cloth painting.

Ask about the medium before assuming how a piece was made. Let the artist name the scene and describe how to read it. We have not assigned a title, individual maker or pigment recipe to the painting in the hero photograph.

sections.title: Meet the place behind the picture

paragraphs.text: Raghurajpur gives this reading a place to continue. The photograph shows an artisan displaying work in a painted doorway. Her name and the precise medium of the piece are not established in the image record; we preserve that uncertainty.

Use the existing Raghurajpur guide for the village’s wider craft and dance connections and practical questions. Arrange any studio visit before setting out; a heritage village is also a place where people live and work.

sections.title: Bring home more than a motif

paragraphs.text: Ask who made the work, what its surface and colours are, and how the artist recommends packing and displaying it. Write down the title or story in the maker’s own words, with their permission.

For a commission, agree the subject, size, price, timescale and delivery before work begins. Ask permission before sharing photographs or reproducing a design. A purchase is an opportunity to learn a person’s name, not just acquire a pattern.
